utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The sudden change of courtroom yesterday afternoon has caused some confusion, but we're now all in Courtroom II. We move into private session to continue to hear the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony is still binding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, having reviewed the transcript yesterday, I'm satisfied I put everything that I needed to put to the witness. There was just one matter that concerned me: Whether Your Honour was clear with the markings on the photograph. I was able to go through the transcript, and it was clear to me, but that's not the test. It was whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- Your Honour was able to -- and Your Honour's colleagues, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I described what I saw as being marked, and I have not been criticised yesterday evening by my colleagues. But if you think there may be any doubt as to whether others would understand it, you're free, then, to ask it to be put on the screen again and to describe in such a way that no one ever could be in doubt as to what is depicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm happy with the answer that Your Honour's given me on the matter. And looking at it, and with the visual image in place, I was satisfied myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at that. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you will be the one who will cross-examine Mr. Bilobrk?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just looking for a little podium, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, you met at the end of August of 2009 with members of the Markac Defence team in Split; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did any member of the Markac team tell you not to speak with any parties -- or to -- to this case or to any authorities regarding the events that occurred during your time in and around Knin in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Franjo Djurica told me that if somebody wanted to talk to me, I should contact him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No member of the team, however, told you not to speak with anyone; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any member of the Markac Defence team, when -- when you met with the Markac Defence team in August of 2009, suggest to you anything that happened in Grubori or what other persons said regarding Grubori or suggested to what you to say about Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Djurica asked you to contact the Markac team if anyone contacted you about the Grubori incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurica asked me to contact him if somebody wanted to talk to me about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you -- I want to focus now on -- on Grubori, August 27th of, 1995, when you were in Grubori performing your function as one of the crime technicians there. When you were in Grubori performing your duties, did Mr. Sacic interfere with your work?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, did he not interfere with my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he or any person in Grubori on August 27th, 1995, issue you any order to do anything in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Sacic, as a member of the special police, have ordered you to conduct any kind of an investigation there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in that way, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mr. Sacic prevent any crime police investigation on that date of the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In your long-time work as a crime technician in the Republic of Croatia, did the special police, to your knowledge, ever conduct any criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that General Markac had anything to do with preventing any kind of a criminal investigations from occurring regarding Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We now know that there was no, at least in August of 1995, specific on-site investigation with a investigating judge and a prosecuting attorney present at the scene. Can you tell us, Mr. Bilobrk, from your position as a crime technician, why there was no on-site investigation in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, who ordered you to go to Grubori on that date?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative duty service of the police, Knin station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a specific person that you recall ordered you to perform your duties on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We report to the duty operations officer. We ask him if there is any information about any bodies that were discovered. And if the answer is yes, if there is, indeed, information, then that person, the duty operations officer, dispatches us to the place where the body was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, who was your immediate superior at that time in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nekic, who was the chief of the crime prevention department in the police administration of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, you and Mr. Vrticevic were both crime technicians on the scene in Grubori in August of 1995. How many other crime technicians were there that would report for duty in the Knin area that you're aware of in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, during the first 15 days, there were five of us. And some 10 or 15 days later, four were sent back to Split, and they were replaced by my colleague Vrticevic, who arrived in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So at least for the time-period of Grubori, was it just the two of you that were the crime technicians for that entire area? In late August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrticevic -- or, Mr. Bilobrk, part of your job, when you are a crime technician, is to note and examine the bodies at a scene and try to make a determination as to, at least visually, how they died. Did you do that in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that at least as far as you were concerned as the person on the scene, a crime technician qualified to do that job, your conclusion at the time was that the persons that you saw in Grubori had died of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So any information that has come out later that a person had their throat cut is simply false; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my professional opinion, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Hedaraly -- yes. I understood that there would be no questions from the Gotovina Defence, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Hedaraly, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Very little, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is something in the transcript I just wanted to clear up at line 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there was something at page 5 as well, if you could look at in one of your questions. But you said line 15 [sic]. Could you tell us what page you are on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Page 6, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 6. "So any information;" is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it came out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, any information that has come out later that a person had their throat cut is incorrect. Is my statement correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps you'd like at page 5, one of the first lines. We now know there is ... that seems to be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that appears from the answer, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked -- part of question was that we now know that there had been no specific on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's then corrected as well. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, in your statement to the Cermak Defence, you described in some detail the procedure by which the operative duty service would be notified and who they would notify and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. And my question for you simply is: At -- that portion of your statement is based on your knowledge as to how the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration functioned; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You don't know exactly what the procedure was or what, in fact, was happening in the Knin Police Station at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And my final question for you is: In all your time in and around Knin, sanitising these bodies, can you give us an estimate on how many bodies that you have sanitised?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't give you an estimate. There is a list. You can obtain the list. It would be hard for me to speak off the top of my head. I can't give you an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would it be more than a hundred?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would it be more than 500?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While I was there, no. I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So somewhere between 100 and 500 is a rough estimate you can give us?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, yesterday on answering a question of Mr. Hedaraly, you mentioned -- the question was: "So let me understand. You heard weapons should be left, and you understood that to mean that weapons should be left in the cars before going to collect the bodies; is that right?" And your answer is: Is that right [sic]. My question is: Why does this question then becomes an argument? Why do you opposed to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was my interpretation. My interpretation of leaving weapons upon the return from Grubori after the job was done in Grubori. That's how I saw the situation, and the reason was the fact that we did not enter the village with long-barrelled rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And yesterday also was discussion about just the wordings "ostaviti" and "postaviti." Ostaviti means "leave as it is." And as far as I understood - please, if I'm wrong, please correct me - but what directly trigger your angerness if you are -- you heard this word "ostaviti," weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get angry. There was no reason for me to get angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that your respond immediately is that you will not do so, anything -- something, that if you -- if somebody wanted to do that, let they do something behind you and not involve you and [indiscernible]. It was your words yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody said that weapons should be left, my profession and my way of thinking and the part of the job that I do is such that on arrival, we don't know -- we didn't know what we could expect in Grubori, what awaited us there. So when somebody mentioned leaving weapons, I automatically reacted. It was my instinct to react. Because I didn't what was happening, whether there had been a war activity, a combat activity, whether somebody had taken weapons during combat and removed it until our arrival, upon which things would be restored to their original state. I didn't know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But as far as I understood from this wording and from Slavonic language, wording "ostaviti" means left without changes, something. It means that it's -- in my understanding, that it's -- if you -- if you are using in your conversation such wording, it means that some weapons should there and you should not take away them when you're doing this on-site -- this criminal technical work. But you mentioned something differently here.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been weapons there. I didn't know what had transpired in Grubori until the moment I arrived Grubori and I saw the bodies. So if the weapons had been by the bodies. If the weapons had been removed to prevent abuse before our arrival and then wanted to restore the situation back to the original by placing weapons back by the dead bodies, in my mind, that would have also constituted a change to the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You're absolute right. But then you -- then you refused that during this conversation word "postaviti" was used; isn't correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leaving. Leaving. To leave. However, the word "to place" also appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, I would like to give some follow-up to the questions put to you by Judge Kinis. Now, what I'd like to know from you, what did you understand to be suggested by that person that spoke? Did you understand that he suggested to leave your own weapons in your cars or to, in one way or another, have weapons being left or placed close or next to the bodies? What was your understanding initially?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding immediately was that the weapons should be left with the dead bodies, and I assumed that there had been fighting there, combat activity, and that someone removed the weapons until we arrived and that then they should be placed back. And that is why I reacted, and I said, There won't be any placing of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this whole story about leaving your weapons in the car, which came up, I think, yesterday, for the first time. I've never heard of it before. Apparently that's not what you thought. But yesterday you presented it as something that you may have understood and in that way. Why do you come up with a totally new version of what you may have understood where, within 24 hours, you take distance from that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a new version at all. Rather, we already discussed yesterday this portion, and my subsequent understanding, upon our return from Grubori, was that that word "leaving the weapons" actually meant that the weapons should be left behind in the cars, because we did not enter the village with long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I believe that is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now, if I understand you well, your initial understanding of what was said was about weapons to be left or placed next to the bodies. And when returning, you thought, Well, they might have meant something different; that is, to leave the weapons in the car. Now, did you tell anyone at a later stage that, having thought over the matter, that you may have misinterpreted and that it was about weapons to be left in the car? Did you tell anyone? Did the tell the court? Did you tell the Prosecution? Did you tell the Cermak Defence? Could you tell us where you presented that second-thought explanation? You don't have to look at anyone else. Mr. -- you don't have to look at anyone else than to me. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've explained this, and I explained it to the Prosecutor as well, and also the -- General Cermak's Defence. And I believe these explanations, and I don't know if they have all been presented in my statements ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I -- let me put to you that I would be surprised that if you would have said this to the Cermak Defence, that they would have failed to put this on paper, because there may have been reasons to put that on paper, but, unless I missed something, they apparently did not.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, really. I should take a look again at the statement that I gave them, to refresh my memory. Maybe it is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, if it would be in the statement, counsel would jump up and say that I would have overlooked something. So, therefore, you don't have to worry about that. Now, I yesterday asked you about your statement given to the Office of the Prosecution. I read it again to you, and it was read to you yesterday as well. "Before any conversation started between the group and me, I heard that someone from the group proposed to someone else something like: Weapons should be placed first. I don't think that [sic] comment was addressed to me but, rather, to another member of the group. It was clear to me that the suggestion I heard was to place guns next to the bodies to make it look as if they put up resistance. I immediately turned and angrily said that there would be no such placing of weapons. I added that if they wanted to do this, they would have done it before coming to me and without my knowledge. My comment stopped any further discussion of placing weapons." Now, that is what you confirmed yesterday as what you said to the interviewer of the Prosecution. A lot of attention has now been paid to the difference between ostaviti or postaviti. You have explained in answer to a question of Judge Kinis that if -- even if the weapons would have been there before, that removing them and then putting them back would be postaviti rather than ostaviti. That's what you testified, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then we should used the word ostaviti, leave. Because if the weapons had already been there, then you should leave them where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you take them away and then place them back, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I just explained. If something was already there and then I removed it and then put it back, that would -- there we would use the word ostaviti, leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check in the transcript of today. May I read your answer to you. "If there had been weapons there. I didn't know what had transpired in Grubori until the moment I arrived Grubori and I saw the bodies. So if the weapons had been by the bodies. If the weapons had been removed to prevent abuse before our arrival and then wanted to restore the situation back to the original by placing weapons back by the dead bodies, in my mind, that would have already [sic] constituted a change to the crime scene." Now, I did understand that the difference between the word ostaviti or ostavite and postavite would be that for ostavite, everything remains unchanged, and for postavite, something is put and that creates a change in the situation. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe we did not explain this quite clearly. Our part of the job entails a lot of situations where the crime scene is changed in various ways. In this particular case where someone had taken the weapons and said it to us, had that been the case, we would have noted that but then we would do our job as usual. We would photograph the bodies. So there wouldn't be any leaving of the weapons there. The weapons had been taken away and then placed back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- what would you have done in a different situation is -- I am focussing on the conversation you had. You explained to us, if I understand well - but please correct me; I am not a linguistic expert - that the difference between ostaviti and postaviti is that in the one situation nothing changed, everything is left as it was, without changes; whereas if you used the word postaviti, that you would change the situation. And you -- in this answer, you clearly explained that removing the weapons and then placing them back already creates a change. Or am I not understanding your answer? I'm just focussing on the words used. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that both on the basis of this answer and on the basis of your description given to the Office of the Prosecution about your reaction, what you immediately thought would be the case, that is, that the guns were not next to the bodies when this discussion took place and that there was a suggestion to put them there, whether or not they had been there before - I leave that apart from this moment - and that you immediately understood that the purpose of it was to make it look as if they put up resistance where that apparently was a false impression. You agree with my analysis of your testimony and of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, for me, it's totally not understandable how, in this context, including your explanation as the difference to ostaviti and postaviti, how the word ostaviti would be better served, the purpose, and -- apart from that, and just -- any statement taken originally in B/C/S, the Chamber would like to have set out. And I tried to do that, but I'm hesitant to do that on my own because I'm not a linguistic expert. Whether in the statements taken originally in B/C/S, for example, Official Notes, court statement, whether the word with a P or without a P is used. Because that means that we know at least how persons who wrote down those statements, how they understood the language used during those interviews. Now, again, whether he has -- had an opportunity to review that, but I would like to see whether there's any -- what it is, with the P or without. Mr. Bilobrk, you were, for a while, together with Mr. Sacic, in a vehicle. You discussed a common acquaintance. Could you tell us, once you arrived in Grubori, did Mr. Sacic stay with you, did he -- when, for example, you went to the bodies, was he with you, or was he not with you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic was with us for part of the time, while we were having this difference with Mr. Cermak about the journalists going to Grubori or not. And then, when we returned from this hamlet, Mr. Sacic was there waiting for us. And then we went back with him together to his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He did not go into the hamlet, into the village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not go into the hamlet with us. Whether he had done it before or whether he did it later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he present when you inspected or photographed or at least when you were close to the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, while we were doing our work, he wasn't anywhere near us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The evidence in respect of where Mr. Sacic was exactly is, to some extent, contradictory. There's evidence saying that he was not present when you looked at the bodies. Others say he entered into the -- into this hamlet and was there when you did your job. Could I again ask you whether Mr. Sacic was close to you when you did your job, that is, to inspect the bodies, photograph them, to do what you had to do with the bodies? I again ask you this question: Whether you're sure that Mr. Sacic was not with you.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were do -- inspecting the bodies, body by body, I did not notice that Mr. Sacic was near us. Whether he was in the village, walking about, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that Mr. Sacic did not enter the hamlet. Why did you positively say he did not, whereas, now you say I didn't see him there? Which is not the same because you said, Whether he was there or not, I don't know. Whereas in your previous answer you said did he not enter the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, but I really did not see Mr. Sacic close to us while we were inspecting the bodies. The only thing that I remember was that we sat in the car together and that we drove to our car, to our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us yesterday that you were angry when you received a copy of the interview you gave to Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic. What did you do? Because what you tell us is that they had written down a completely false or at least a substantially false statement. What action did you take once you had received that -- what you said was a largely false statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean toward Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic? Or are you referring to one of the investigators of the OTP? I apologise, I didn't understand your question. What did you mean by what did I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at a rather late stage, you see that a false statement is put on paper; a copy is given to you; you are angry. What action did you take to whomever to have that re-addressed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a copy of the statement only when I met the gentleman from the Prosecution, and I only had an opportunity to see it. I didn't get it. And I said to the Prosecutor that that portion of the interview was incorrect -- or statement was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what action did you take against Mr. Gerovac and Mr. Mikulic? Did you complain at the chiefs, or did you say, This is a shame. Taking false statements is not something I -- I accept or ... Or did you just leave it as it was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with Mr. Gerovac and Mikulic. I just let things go as they did ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... didn't write a letter, Please be informed that I became aware that a false statement is put on paper; it doesn't reflect the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilobrk, you're a police officer. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as -- if a statement is taken from you and is put on paper in a rather false way, that you just leave it to that? And with all the possible negative consequences for others, you just leave that as it is?

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I really didn't give it much thought. I didn't think about that. Today I would act differently. But, at that moment, I didn't think of that. And this involved colleagues. And I assume that if they had done their job and if they had written something down, that they should have done it in a proper way and accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. But those were your inner thoughts which were not communicated with their chiefs, with the court. You didn't say to the court, Well, I know it cannot be used in evidence, but please be aware that I never said what -- you didn't go to the court at any moment and ...

utterances.speaker: JOZO BILOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, at the time, in the court, I didn't know about the statement that they had written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you didn't go back to the court later and say, I only now found out ... Let's leave it as it is. That's -- your answer's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While Your Honour is just thinking, a matter: You asked over the use of the word ostaviti. I don't know if that would help for me to direct Your Honour there if Your Honour wanted to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it is more -- for me it's not -- I looked at the 9th of November statement where I thought, but that's exactly the reason why I'm seeking your confirmation, that I thought that "postave" is used. I looked at the statement given before the court, and I think I found that postaviti was used, but it's all reconstruction. I'd rather have a full list of the use of the words postaviti and ostaviti. And if the parties could agree on that, I don't think that that should be a matter of dispute. And if there is any dispute, we'll find the linguistic experts to -- or at least those who are native speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I had found it our statement, though, when Your Honour mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to have it for all the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- and ... Then I have no further questions. Have my questions triggered any need for further questions? And same too for Judge Kinis's questions. Then, Mr. Bilobrk, this concludes your testimony. I would to thank you for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I would like you to remain stand by during the day. We'll hear some other evidence as well. This is - I'm not saying we will - but there is a chance that we may need to put further questions to you on the basis of what we'll hear further. Therefore, I would like to ask you to remain stand by during the day. VWS, the Victims and Witness Section, will take care of you. And you're instructed not to speak with anyone about your testimony which you've given, in view of the fact that there may be - I'm not saying there will be - but there may be a follow-up. Therefore, the instruction is the same: Once we have concluded the hearings today, you'll receive a message whether you are free, then, to speak again with whomever you want about your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to invite the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, for the next witness, the Chamber has no information as to whether any protective measures are sought by that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: None are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None are. Nevertheless, we'll hear the testimony in private session, as we did yesterday. And most likely we'll lift the confidentiality rather soon. And we'll have to wait until the witness is brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, the Prosecution will call Witness 178 before 177. And I think it is going to become clear why during the examination. It is going to be Mr. Mikulic and then Mr. Gerovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Mikulic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mikulic. I'm the one who is speaking, although you receive my words in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Mikulic. Mr. Mikulic, just to be sure that you understand the present situation, you have not asked for any protective measures. Nevertheless, we hear your evidence in private session. Most likely your evidence will be public very soon, but in order to protect the integrity of the evidence and the proceedings, the Chamber has decided that, today, we'll hear your evidence without the outside world knowing about it already. But it's our firm expectation, since you did not ask for protective measures, that it will be public in a matter of days. You will now first be examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you first please state your full name and your date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Mikulic, born on the 31st of October, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I'm a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Who is your employer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior, the police administration of Zagreb, the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Starting in 2009, were you involved in the investigation of the killings in Grubori that occurred in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, What is your role in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, in the course of September 2009 at the level of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, the administration of crime prevention police decided to set up a task force, pursuant to the minister's decision, with a goal to investigate the killing of Serbian civilians in Grubori which took place on the 25th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, as part of this investigation, did you interview two forensic technicians in November 2009, Mr. Jozo Bilobrk and Mr. Ivica Vrticevic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrticevic? Not Krsticevic; Vrticevic. Mr. Jozo Bilobrk and Mr. Ivica Vrticevic were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There may have just have been an issue with interpretation, but I think the record is clear that you interviewed both Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic in November 2009.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Myself and my colleague from the police, Antonio Gerovac, interviewed the two of them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, when you interviewed Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic, they had already been interviewed by other officers of the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that they were interviewed on two occasions before that. Mr. Robert Badzim from the police administration of Knin spoke to them. He was also a member of the task force that was set up pursuant to the decision of the head of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Court what led you to re-interview Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic? And just so you know, I'm treating them together for now just to be more efficient. Whenever you feel it's better to separate them, we can deal with them one at a time. So can you tell us what led you to re-interview these two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the first interview carried out by our colleague, Robert Badzim, with Ivica Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk took place on the 12th of October, 2009. The interview with the two of them was recorded on one Official Note which is inadmissible in the police practice. Normally interviews are carried out separately, and every interview has to be covered by a separate Official Note. That's -- that was the first reason. The second reason was the fact that - I don't know whether you have that Official Note - in the introduction to that Official Note, our colleague Badzim stated that our colleagues Vrticevic and Bilobrk somehow stated that they did not intend to say anything, any of the details about the sanitisation of the terrain in Grubori in 1995, because they had already been interviewed, as they said, by the representatives of the Defence teams of Croatian Generals. And it was suggested that any information that they might have might harm the Defence of the Croatian generals. Mr. Badzim said it himself that they were not very forthcoming during the interview. They just provided very general information about their participation in the event and in the sanitisation of the terrain. After that, at the level of the ministry, our colleague Badzim was requested to repeat the interviews in order to establish everything that was necessary to proceed with the criminal investigation. After that, he compiled two separate Official Notes, but the contents thereof remained the same. Nothing changed with regard to the contents of those Official Notes. After that, in November --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I can just stop you here just so that we go -- we go piece by piece. I just want to show you these Official Notes so you can confirm to the Court that these are the ones you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we have P2731 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like counsel to point out in this P2731 where - anywhere in this Official Note - it is suggested that the Defence teams --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr -- Mr. -- that's not what I understand. The only thing Mr. Hedaraly is doing is verifying with the witness whether the Official Notes he spoke about -- whether that are the Official Notes which Mr. Hedaraly will show to him. That's what is done by Mr. Hedaraly at this moment. And if you want to further explore the content of the Official Notes, then that can be done at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to make it perfectly clear. I don't want any suggestions -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- but -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kuzmanovic, what you would not like. Wait -- first of all, you intervene when Mr. Hedaraly is just asking for a document to be brought on the screen where he clearly has explained what his purpose is. That is, to see whether the document on the screen is the Official Note the witness talked about. That's perfectly right. There was no reason to intervene. If at any stage Mr. Hedaraly will suggest something which you think would be inappropriate, then you may rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that under the present circumstances Mr. Hedaraly will be very cautious not to create a situation in which you feel that you should rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, on the screen now is an Official Note which is an Official Note which has both Mr. Vrticevic's and Mr. Bilobrk's names as the people that are interviewed. If you want to look at the second page as well, we can do so. Can you confirm that this is the first Official Note that you were talking about where you said that they were both interviewed -- that there was one Official Note created for both interviewees?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one, written on two pages. But that's the Official Note that was compiled by our colleague Badzim, the first Official Note that he ever compiled. And what I was talking about and why it was necessary to repeat the interviews, you will find that in the first paragraph. Or, rather, in the second paragraph. Because of the circumstances that took place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast. It is impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, if you read, for the interpreters to be able to read at an appropriate pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd also ask that the witness be directed to answer the question that's asked and not go beyond the scope of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, if the witness goes beyond the scope of the question and if Mr. Hedaraly thinks that useful information may come up, then he either can stop the witness and say that this goes beyond his question or he can let it go. If this would result in receiving irrelevant information resulting in a waste of time, then, of course, the Chamber will intervene as well. Mr. Kuzmanovic, the intervening at appropriate moments on appropriate matters is fully accepted by the Chamber. Your last interventions were of a kind where there can be some doubt, if not serious doubt, as to the appropriateness of it or not. I would like to ask you to carefully consider when you intervene again. Mr. Hedaraly, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to state something for the record. I'm protecting the interests of my client. And if the Court feels that that's something that's unnecessary or doesn't like it, I'm sorry. I'm defending the interests of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic, no one doubts that you are defending the interests of your client. That is not the same as doing what you wish to do if the Court considers it inappropriate. It's finally the Court which allows you, and I did it in very gentle way, I would say. I said that we fully accept interventions but that the interventions, until now, were not of a kind which would have been placed where the Court was convinced that they were appropriately placed. We didn't do anything else. And have to accept that for the time being. Mr. Hedaraly can continue. What I want to prevent is that by too many interventions - and I let it go for the first one or two, to find out what they were - that the flow of evidence is interrupted in a way which -- in which it should not be interrupted. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, before you were interrupted. You wanted to point out something in this Official Note related to what you had stated earlier today in your testimony. Can you please tell us which portion you're referring us to. And if you want to read from it, please do so slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't need to read it. We'll find it in the first two paragraphs. And that was the main reason why there was a request to repeat the interview, to clarify those circumstances and to establish all the important facts. It was inadmissible for Mr. Vrticevic and for Mr. Bilobrk to remain active police officers and behave in that way. It was not up to them to decide what to say, what not to say, what to cover up, what not to cover up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were two other Official Notes taken by Mr. Badzim. Let me show those to you and you can confirm that these are the ones you were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: First, if we can have P2730, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first one, covering the interview with Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then if we can have 65 ter 7570, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the second one. This is the second Official Note that my colleague Mr. Gerovac and myself created. There should be another Official Note created by my colleague Mr. Badzim after the interview with Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct. And just give me one moment and I we will find the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We'll get it at a later stage. There was a confused -- a confusion. So we'll review that one a little later. I apologise for that. Now, when you re-interviewed Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic, did you come into possession of any new information that you thought would be relevant in those interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, our primary task was to clarify their position as to why they didn't want to talk about what they knew about the incident in Grubori. And in that sense, we invited them to provide the information they had and to explain the roles they played in the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you interview anyone else that gave you any information about what Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic may know that they did not say in their first interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Before that, we interviewed -- or, rather, I and my colleague Nikola Ilijas, who was also a member of that task force, we interviewed Mr. Franjo Djurica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did Mr. -- well, why did you interview Mr. -- Mr. Franjo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the -- according to the plan of our crime investigation. Mr. Djurica, at the time, in the course of 1995, was the chief of the police sector with the Ministry of the Interior, and he was in charge of coordinating the activities in the then-liberated areas -- area on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior, in order to establish and control the work of the police. There was a need to interview him and to gather any information that he might have been in possession of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did he give you any information relating to Grubori that you found to be relevant?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when the official part of the interview was over, Mr. Franjo Djurica, at the very beginning of the interview, said that he could only provide information about Grubori that he had had at the time, when this -- he discharged those duties. And that was primarily for the fact that in the course of 2005, at the level of the MUP, a commission was set up. He was the president of that commission. And that commission was responsible, according to him, responsible for the defence of the generals who were standing trial before the international Tribunal. When he started working in that commission, after that, his information about the events expanded because he had had an opportunity to read a lot more documents that he wasn't even aware of in 1995. And at the end of -- the interview was conducted, it was completed, and Mr. Djurica told us what he knew in 1995. And when the interview was over, when it was completed, Mr. Ilijas and myself asked him if it was true that they had spoken to Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic and whether it was true that they had told him that they had suggested that should anybody want to talk to them, they shouldn't say what they knew. Mr. Djurica replied that as a professional he should not answer that question but as a former -- former colleague and professional, he valued our efforts and our work and that he therefore would say that he did talk to them. But he never suggested that they should cover up anything. His only suggestion was that should anybody wanted to talk to them, that he should be made aware of that in order to know what position to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did he you tell you anything about these interviews that he conducted with Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djurica was asked a concrete question, and that was whether he was able to reveal the information that they were in possession of. And after a short pause, he -- Mr. Djurica said that what he was going to tell us then we should consider as never having been told to us and that he would never confirm that he had ever stated that. He said that, in the course of the interview that he conducted in the -- in the course of August with Mr. Vrticevic and Bilobrk, that they had stated before him that there had been proposals, certain proposals, on the part of some high MUP and HV officials that the crime scene in Grubori should be altered in the following way: That weapons should be placed by the dead bodies in order to make it appear as if there had been an armed conflict, fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you ask him who he [Realtime transcript read in error "you"] understood to have made these proposals?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: We did ask him who could be most harmed by that information, whether it's known who the proposals came from. Mr. Djurica says that Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic told him that the proposal had come from General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, page 33, line 5, it's my recollection that you said: "Did you ask him who 'he' understood to have made these proposals?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you -- did you record this information that Mr. Franjo gave you in the Official Note of the interview that you prepared of Mr. Franjo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurica asked us not to record that in the Official Note. He said that he would deny ever having said that, should he be asked about that. When we returned to our workplaces, during our briefing, daily briefing session, we reported back to the task force, and an operative report was compiled about that. I must admit that we took it with a grain of salt because there were a lot of contradictions in the statements of Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk. We did not assign too much value to the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 7640 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will ask to you confirm that this is the Official Note of the interview that you prepared with Mr. Franjo. We can also look at the last page whenever you are ready.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think this is the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have 65 ter 7640 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P2733. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2733 is admitted into evidence. And as far as confidentiality is concerned, the same applies as yesterday. As long as the confidentiality of this hearing has not yet been lifted, the confidentiality of these documents should be observed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, let me now try to, again, get the -- the Official Note of Mr. Vrticevic that was prepared after the joint interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is it. I believe Mr. Badzim has drafted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we can see that's Mr. Badzim --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 7569 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P2734. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2734 is admitted into evidence. Same ruling in relation to confidentiality. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, do you know why Mr. Franjo shared this information with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that he felt he should, since that question had already been put to him, whether it was true that they had discussed and whether -- and what he would say if somebody asked him to repeat that. So he felt, as a former policeman, the need to describe -- to explain this. But he also said that in view of the fact that he was a member of the team and president of that committee, he would never officially confirm that he had actually said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I now want to move to the interviews that you and your colleague conducted with Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that the schedule is for the break to be in ten minutes. I don't know if you wish me to start this topic now or if you would prefer to take an earlier break so that we have it all in one -- I leave it to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be perhaps better if we move subject, to not interrupt it, after ten minutes and have a break. The only concern I may have, that is, we have an early break -- no, the problem is that the tape for the second round would be too short to cover it, so we would then have a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One tape would not cover a lengthy second session. Therefore, you're invited to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were both Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk interviewed the same day by you and your colleague Mr. Gerovac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the same day. I believe it was on the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you interview them together or separately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Separately. With each one of them, we had separate interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Who did you interview first?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think with interviewed first Mr. Vrticevic in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And -- and when did you interview Mr. Bilobrk, and where did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: After that, at the police administration building, the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration building, and we conducted the interview with Mr. Bilobrk there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vrticevic's office, where you conducted his interview, in the same building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the premises of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration. I believe this was in the crime prevention department where he works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you know -- let me first start with your interview with Mr. Bilobrk. Did you know Mr. Bilobrk from before, before that day, when you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was your interview with Mr. Bilobrk a formal interview or an informal interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: It was a formal interview, an official interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "a formal interview"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: An interview that was conducted as part of a criminal investigation. It wasn't conducted on a sort of personal basis or private basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Bilobrk that this would -- that this was a formal interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Of course, he knew that. And his superiors had been informed that we would come to interview him. We had announced our arrival. This was announced by the crime police department that we would come and conduct interviews with Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you drive down from Zagreb for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember how the interview started? Can you tell the Court how the interview with Mr. Bilobrk started; if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember the details, but it proceeded without any glitches. It was very casual. We explained the reasons for our coming there and that we need to clarify these details that we had an interest in. The interview proceeded quite casually and professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what questions or what -- what question did you put -- what was the first question that you put to Mr. Bilobrk; if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely, but we told him what we wanted to discuss. In other words, the events in Grubori. And we wanted to ask him about what he knew about the events. And I believe that the first question was for him to tell us everything he knew about it, about what had happened there, and to explain what his role in the events was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when he answered this first series of question [sic] that you asked him, did he say anything to you about what you had learned from Mr. Franjo about the proposals to alter the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: He confirmed that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember what specific question you asked him in order for him to confirm that? Did you present that information to him? Did he tell him what it was, who you got it from? We're trying to get a picture of how this interview developed and how that information came about.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. We did not indicate to him at first that we had already interviewed Mr. Djurica, or talked with Mr. Djurica. We asked him, in view of what he had said in his first Official Note, to tell us about the knowledge that he had that he thought might be harmful, what that knowledge was. And we told him that this was a serious criminal investigation and that Croatian generals were being tried for it and that the only purpose of the interview of the -- was to establish the truth. And then he began to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did he then right away tell you about the -- these proposals, to alter the crime scene by placing weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. He began to -- describing that immediately, how the whole thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did he name the person or persons who had made these proposals?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And who did he name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: He named -- he said that General Cermak had come to him and suggested that a criminal investigation be conducted and that weapons be placed by the bodies in order to make it appear as if there had been fighting and this to be done before journalists who would witness it. And he opposed that. He said that his reaction had been rather indignant, vehement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you, in your questions, suggest to him that General Cermak may have made such proposals?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, we were discussing the interview that you and Mr. Gerovac conducted with Mr. Bilobrk in November 2009. And we were talking about General Cermak being mentioned. And I just need to ask you this, to be sure: Are you absolutely certain that it is Mr. Bilobrk who first stated that General Cermak was the person who made these proposals, to place weapons next to bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Bilobrk said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to make this perfectly clear, Mr. Mikulic, there are several ways in which you can introduce that matter. You can say, We heard about suggestions of changing the crime scene. And if you do that and if then someone's come with the story of what was suggested, then you haven't given much clues. You can also introduce the matter by saying, We were informed that it was suggested that weapons would be put or should be left close to the bodies and then that someone, in response, tells you who suggested that. Of course, a third way of introducing the matter is to say, We received information that it was suggested at that place by Mr. Cermak or by Mr. Sacic -- by whomever, and if you give all the clues. Now I'd like to know exactly what clues you had given to Mr. Bilobrk when you interviewed him, because I do understand that you had received information. Was he the first who stated that it was suggested that weapons be put next to the bodies; or did you seek confirmation, telling him that you'd received information that it was suggested that weapons should be put next to the bodies? Do you remember whether it was him or you who first mentioned weapons to be put next to the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is best to look at the Official Note. I cannot really be terribly precise because some seven or eight months have elapsed since. But I think that it was very well described in the Official Note how this whole interview proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we'll have a look at the Official Note and see whether question and answer are clearly described. And, of course, we do not know yet whether that's the complete question or not. Now, same question: Was it Mr. Bilobrk that first mentioned Mr. Cermak as the one who may have suggested to change the crime scene; or did you mention Mr. Cermak as the one who would have suggested to do so and that he confirmed? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not suggest anything or who this was about. We suggested, if I recall, whether there were any suggestions or proposals by anyone, without mentioning any names, that something be done or not be done on site at the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without yet telling what to be done to the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we never mentioned specifically what it was. We did have certain facts, but we did not want to put leading questions. We wanted him to describe what he knew about the events. And I remember that toward the end of this interview we asked him whether what he had just told us was the knowledge that he also provided when he was interviewed by Mr. Franjo Djurica, and he confirmed. This was the -- a question that we put at the end of this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to follow up on the Judge's question, let's have P2732 on the screen, which is the Official Note of interview. 2732. Is there a technical problem? I can -- we can come back to it later if it would be better -- yeah? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There's a technical problem, Mr. Mikulic. We'll look at the note in just a few -- a few -- hopefully minutes. Did you take any notes during that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Notes are taken. This is standard. Notes are taken during an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to be completely clear, I mean handwritten notes at the same time; not the Official Note that is typed up later on.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, handwritten notes too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember if both you and Mr. Gerovac took handwritten notes during that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think that it was only Mr. Gerovac who took handwritten notes. I'm pretty certain. We conducted the interview jointly. We were both present. But I think - and I'm pretty sure - that he was the one who took notes on both these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that -- is that the standard practice that only one of the interviewers would take handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: It is standard practice that one would take notes. That the person who begins with questions and begins the interview, that that same person takes notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what is the procedure for compiling the Official Note of interview? First of all, generally. What would be the general procedure for compiling the Official Note of an interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the time available. We would either compile it on the same day, type it into a computer, or we would use a typist, an official typist, who would type it for us. In this case, Mr. Gerovac and I did it ourselves. And judging by the style, I believe it was Mr. Gerovac who compiled. But I was there with him, and then we both signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review the note before signing it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the rule. You have to read the note and then if there are any suggestions or any disagreements or doubts in the interpretation of the interview, we would check the notes again and those corrections would be made. And then in the end, when the note is completed, then we would both sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you signed the Official Note, does that mean that you are satisfied that it accurately reflects what happened in the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what happens to the handwritten notes that have been made at the time of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, we keep them for a while with us. If we take it down in a notebook, we keep it for a while. And then -- well, some people would keep all those notes, others would dispose of them. But there is no legal obligation to keep them or that they be attached as part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: During your interview with Mr. Bilobrk, did you -- did you or your colleague light up a cigarette close to the window of the room where you had the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I lit up a cigarette. And, I believe, Mr. Bilobrk too, because he is a smoker too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How long did that interview last?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: It is hard to say as I sit here now, but I believe that it couldn't have lasted more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we have --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I believe that with Mr. Vrticevic it was a bit shorter; at most, half an hour. Where the interview of Mr. Bilobrk lasted about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have the Official Note on the screen now, which is P2732. And we see here that the interview was conducted on 5 November, as you had stated, and that the note was made on the 9th of November. Now, noting that the 5th of November, 2009, was a Thursday and the 9 of November was a Monday, is that a usual delay between the interview and the Official Note being prepared?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, in essence, as I said, we prepare an Official Note on the same day, as a rule, or on the next day, at the latest. But this one was drafted some four days later, and the reason was that we were actually on an official trip. We were away from our offices. We spoke with Mr. Bilobrk on Thursday, I believe. We were in Split. And on Friday we already had a new interview or interviews to conduct in Zadar, also to do with Grubori. And then we returned home late that evening. So the first next business day we exactly compiled the Official Note. We did not have occasion during those two days to draft the Official Note because he was not the only person we interviewed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we look at the Official Note, and can you tell us if it reflects accurately the questions that were put to Mr. Bilobrk and his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we move down in the English a little bit on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And there's quite a long statement about the need for another interview and that new facts have been established which -- I lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was fine before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "New facts have been established which suggest that during the first preliminary interview conducted with him on 13 October 2009, he did not provide all the facts in his possession regarding the -- that event, the above was asked if it had been suggested to him and to his colleague Ivica Vrticevic, who was working with him as a crime technician on the humane clearing up of the dead bodies of civilians killed in the village of Grubori, by somebody from the then-senior commanding structures of the MUP or the Ministry of Defence that they should have conducted an on-site investigation in the village of Grubori but that before that they should have placed guns next to the ... bodies of civilians who had been killed in order to make it" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "...make it appear" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we have the full page, please, on the screen. That's going to be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "... make it appear as if they had put up resistance to member of special police, the above stated that the day when they went to Grubori in order to carry out the humane clearing up process, sometime in the morning, General Cermak came in front of the Knin Police Administration building escorted by a few soldiers from his security" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Please turn the page in English and have the original -- the first page back on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "He remembers that when Cermak arrived, he was sitting on the stairs with several colleagues whose name he does not now remember anymore but he allows for the possibility that among them there was, on that occasion, his colleague Ivica Vrticevic. When Cermak came to them, he said that an on-site investigation had to be conducted in Grubori but that before the on-site investigation, guns had to be placed next to the ... bodies in order to make it appear as if the persons killed had put up resistance. He remembers that he got angry at Cermak's suggestion and told him that he would not do that, and if they had intentions of doing something like that, that he did not want to know anything about it nor did he want to participate in it. Cermak did not comment his reaction; he just turned around and left." Now, my question for you, Mr. Mikulic, and it goes back to what the Presiding Judge asked you earlier: Do you remember if this is how the question and answer proceeded, that there was -- that you did put to Mr. Bilobrk that there was a suggestion by a high-level official and, according to this note, that Mr. Bilobrk volunteered the name of Mr. Cermak; or was it in some other way that the questioning occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: It was just as it is described in here. In that conversation, we were not the ones who mentioned the person's name. However, based on the question, we made him aware that we have some facts available to us. We did not suggest the answer to him. We wanted to hear it from him.
