Not for a single moment did we make any suggestions as to the possible name that we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is it the current practice or the common practice to try and convey as accurately as possible what happened in the interview, including the sequence of any possible questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've let it go for quite some time because I didn't want to interrupt the flow but we've had -- this is a very leading question. And we've had, before the previous question, several leading questions. And I would just ask that no leading questions be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We could rephrase the question, Mr. Hedaraly. You asked the witness whether it's the current practice to convey as accurately as possible or not to convey as accurately as possible what happened in the interview. That is -- that would satisfy -- Could you tell us whether it's common practice to convey as accurately as possible what happened in the interview or not to convey as accurately as possible what happened in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The practice and the obligation is to make the personal note reflect as accurately as possible what the person stated. And it is in the third person, singular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one question in this respect for you. I asked you a couple of minutes ago -- and let me first start with one of your answers. You said: "We suggested, if I recall, whether there were any suggestions or proposals by anyone, without mentioning any names, that something be done or not be done on the site at the crime scene." And then I asked you: "Yes. Without yet telling what to be done to the crime scene?" And then you answered. You said: "No, we never mentioned specifically what it was. We did have certain facts, but we did not want to put leading questions." Now, the way in which it's written down, as just read by Mr. Hedaraly, suggests that you put to Mr. Bilobrk that it was not just something to be done at the crime scene but that it was weapons to be put or to be left next to the bodies. That's -- you asked us to look at the language used in the Official Note. And, similarly, the language suggests that without giving a name, you, nevertheless, hinted at high officials. Now, did you tell Mr. Bilobrk or did you mention first weapons to be put or left next to the bodies? And did you mention first that it was high officials? Or did he come up, without you having told him, the detail of weapons next to the bodies; that's the first part of the question. And, second, whether it would be - although not giving names - but it would be high officials which would have suggested that? Could you answer that question. It's a long question. If you wanted me to summarise it, I will be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the interview, the questions were put exactly in the way -- in the way as reflected in here. We did not mention any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the question was put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you did mention, before Mr. Bilobrk said anything about it, about weapons to be placed or left next to the bodies. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's in the Official Note, then I'm sure that the question was worded exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were the first one who referred to high officials, although not naming any of them. Is that also correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can't be sure whether it was myself or my colleague Mr. Gerovac. The question was put in the sense as to whether it was a high official of the MUP or a high official of the Ministry of Defence who may have suggested something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did the fact that this was the third time that Mr. Bilobrk was going to be interviewed by the MUP affect, in any way, your questioning or the way you conducted the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. We wanted to clarify and collect all information that Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic had. We just wanted to put a closure on all that, to see what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you -- did you pressure Mr. Bilobrk in any way during that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mikulic, Mr. Bilobrk has testified in this court, and he categorically denied telling you that General Cermak told him to place weapons next to the bodies in Grubori. Do you have any -- any comment or any response to this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: My response is that he is not telling the truth. He did say that during the interview, and that's how it was recorded in the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me just briefly tell you another thing Mr. Bilobrk said in his testimony, and I ask to you comment on it. It starts at page 28724, line 25. And the question that was put to Mr. Bilobrk was: "Had you ever said to them" -- meaning to you and Mr. Mikulic, "that General Cermak had suggested placing guns next to the bodies at Grubori?" Mr. Bilobrk responded: "No. They came to me with that information. That's what they suggested." Then the question: "And how did they suggest that to you? Describe what happened in the time you spent with them. How did they suggest it?" Mr. Bilobrk answered: "During that conversation, or while we conversed, rather, I can't remember which one of them mentioned that first. I can't repeat the words verbatim. "In any case, what they said was this. We came by information that General Cermak offered, or suggested, that you should place weapons by the dead bodies." The question was: "And what did you say to that, when that was stated by one of them?" And Mr. Bilobrk answered: "I told them that Mr. Cermak never said that to me, and it would have been strange if a person whom I saw for the first time among a group of people to say that to me. It would have been totally strange and didn't make much sense to imagine that somebody I saw for the first time came up to me and said, Take weapons and place them by dead bodies." Now, this is what Mr. Bilobrk stated to this Chamber about what happened in that interview. Can you tell us if that did happen in that interview, the way he described it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. When we spoke to him, we asked him how come that Mr. Cermak, while you were sitting in front of the police station, that it was nobody else but you that he should address? And he said that somebody from the police administration or from the police station told him who he was and to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. Could you please restart your answer. And do it slowly so that not only interpreters but also those who are transcribing your words can put them in full accuracy in the computer system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the interview, we asked Mr. Bilobrk - and I remember that well - how come that General Cermak had known that he should address him as a person who would be carrying out the on-site investigation. Mr. Bilobrk answered that Mr. Cermak had been advised to do so by a member of staff or the head of either the police administration or the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bilobrk [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would -- that seems not to be the right person to address at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mikulic, my mistake. Mr. Mikulic, let me ask you, what would you have to gain by recording false information in an Official Note like this one?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now briefly conclude. We discussed the interview you had with Mr. Vrticevic the same day. And I think you mentioned that it was in his office on the same day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember that interview and how Mr. Vrticevic -- how -- let me restate my question. Do you remember how that interview proceeded and whether that issue of the guns being placed next to the bodies was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: The same question was put to Mr. Vrticevic. And it was worded more or less in the same way. Mr. Vrticevic was a bit more arrogant, if I may put it that way. He was a bit more temperamental in that interview. And his position was still that he shouldn't be talking to us, that he had already stated whatever he knew, that he did not intend to go over the same ground again. And then we let him know that he was also a police officer just like us and that he should not be behaving in that way, and if he had any information to share, that he should come forth in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you the Official Note of that interview which we had seen earlier inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 7570.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I had not read the whole portion on the record. We can see at the bottom in the English, when it's going to come up, that the similar question to the one we just saw in Mr. Bilobrk's Official Note is present. I'll just leave it on the screen for a few seconds so everyone can read it and spare the interpreters and the transcriber me reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go completely at the bottom of the English -- can we just have the page, if possible, so everyone can read it in one dimension -- no, both the English and the B/C/S side by side. Can we have the B/C/S in a manner that the witness could read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the answer of Mr. Vrticevic to the similar question that you put to him at the bottom in the English is: "The interviewed person at first categorically denied such a possibility, but after a short time he said that he was not able to" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "... remember exactly."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the English only turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "... but that did he allow for the possibility that at that time someone might have suggested something like this [sic] however, due to the lapse of time, he was currently unable to remember those details. "To the specific question whether such suggestion had come from Zeljko Sacic or from General Ivan Cermak, the interviewed person stated that he was unable to give an accurate answer to that question and he [sic] repeated that he was unable to remember that." Now, Mr. Mikulic, is that you how remember the questioning of Mr. Vrticevic? You first asked him about the suggestion of placing weapons by a high-level official. And when he said that he could not remember, then you suggested some specific names to him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the interview, he was evasive. He tried to avoid answering the question. And finally he said that there was such a possibility but he did not remember after such a long time. And then concrete names were given to him. The names were General Cermak or Mr. Sacic. And even after that, his answer was that after such a long time he could not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I just show you the last page so that you can confirm that you have signed this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have 65 ter 7570 in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2735. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2735 is admitted into evidence. Just for my understanding, Mr. Mikulic, the course of the interview with Mr. Bilobrk was therefore different as far as just as suggesting names, compared to the interview with Mr. Vrticevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Bilobrk was more forthcoming, more communicative, and more accessible during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay, you will be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first questions I want to ask you about, Mr. Mikulic, is this: When you interviewed Mr. Djurica, you didn't include in that Official Note of interview the allegation about reconstructing the crime scene that he made to you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were investigating a serious crime on behalf of your government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why, then, did you not put into your Official Note information that you had been given that was important to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Because Mr. Djurica insisted that that should not be recorded in the original part of the note. But let me say that an Official Note was compiled about that information. It was submitted. What I'm saying is that it did not remain hanging in the air. An Official Note was indeed compiled, and it must be part of our file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the Official Note that we have looked at was made, and it's our Exhibit P2733, but there is nothing in that Official Note about this information Franjo Djurica gave you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I repeat, Mr. Djurica said that he had obtained that information as a member and the head of the commission. Therefore, he would never confirm that he knew anything about that. And he insisted that it should not make part of the Official Note. We could not let it hang in the air, and that's why a separate, special Official Note was compiled. It was a written note -- actually, it was not an Official Note; it was just a report that was compiled which contained that particular information, and it was submitted to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So why could Franjo Djurica tell you what should or should not be included within the Official Note that you were taking as part of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurica did not dictate what could be recorded and what couldn't be. After the official part of the interview was over, he stated what he did. He is a policeman, and he was aware of the principle that we followed in our actions. And he asked us, he requested, that that part of the interview, after the official part was over, not become part of the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, he was telling you what could or could not be included in the note, wasn't he? And you followed his instruction, apparently.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: He just requested. He asked us not to put that into the Official Note. And after that, we created an official report. He only requested kindly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I ask about that. But I now want to go on to your interviews with Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic. The first person you interviewed on that day was Mr. Vrticevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that that was the sequence: Mr. Vrticevic first and then Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, who took notes of that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was my colleague, Mr. Antonio Gerovac, who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, why -- why do you believe it was your colleague, Mr. Antonio Gerovac? It was either one or other of you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Because on that day we had already had some interviews and I was the one who took notes on those. I believe that we had some interviews in Knin and then in Split, and I believe that I had already had those interviews and made notes. So it would not have been fair for the same person to make all the notes. It was only fair for the person who had not made notes previously to take the duty over during the later stage of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So just to make it clear: You did not make the notes in relation to Mr. Vrticevic's interview.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, not me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to Mr. Bilobrk's interview, you did not take notes of his interview.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I did not. It was my colleague, Mr. Gerovac. Are you referring to the handwritten notes which were taken during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: When you are just putting -- when you're jotting down notes on a piece of paper, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was my colleague Mr. Gerovac. I'm almost absolutely sure that it was him on both occasions during both of the relevant interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're almost absolutely sure. All I need to know is whether you took any notes at the time. Did you or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you seen those notes at all recently? When did you last see them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: When we compiled this Official Note, that is when my colleague Mr. Gerovac had them before him. So this was - let's see - seven months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And after the interview that you've taken, is it right that you don't show the notes of the interview to the person you've interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. Do we show the handwritten notes to the person we are interviewing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll -- I'll rephrase it. After you have interviewed Mr. Vrticevic and you've written the Official Note, did you show him what you had written?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The same question in relation to Mr. Bilobrk: Did you show him what you had written in the Official Note after you had written it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. Nor do we have that obligation under our laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like us now to look at Mr. Vrticevic's interview, Official Note, which has just been given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: P2734 -- 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This Official Note records that you were asking him questions about the death of Serb civilians in Grubori, which has led to new information; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you told him he hadn't provided all the information he had about what had happened; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You then asked, according to this note, whether someone from senior leading structures of the Ministry of Interior or Ministry of Defence had suggested to him and his colleague and essentially it goes on to say about constructing a crime scene. Is that how you say this interview happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. As it is written down here, that's how the question was phrased by Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So why were you suggesting first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I have difficulties in -- you say: "As it is written down here, that's how the question was phrased by Mr. Vrticevic." May I take it that you said, How the question was phrased that was put to Mr. Vrticevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Put to Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, because he wasn't giving you this information, was he? You were suggesting information to him. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: We weren't suggesting anything to him. We just asked him during this interview to tell us about what he knew that he had already conveyed to Mr. Franjo Djurica, and we asked him to tell us about it because he kept repeating that he didn't want to speak about that because that could be harmful to the generals' Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, are you saying he was interviewed by Franjo Djurica? Are you saying that that was the basis of your questioning, that he was interviewed by Franjo Djurica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, during the first interview conducted by Mr. Badzim, Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk said that they had already provided their statements to the team for the Defence for -- of the general and that that they had spoken with Mr. Franjo Djurica and that he had told him that if anyone asked them to interview them, that he should inform him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, where is it in this Official Note that you were asking him about what he had told Franjo Djurica? For a start. Where does it say that here? It doesn't, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you told the Court earlier today that the purpose of your interviews was not to suggest answers to people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, here you are suggesting that something happened in Grubori, that a suggestion was made to him and his colleague to create the crime scene. That's what you're suggesting to him, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I have already said that Mr. Vrticevic was more temperamental during this interview, and I have to say he was also a bit more arrogant. And when we started the interview, he was told that we were going to discuss specific issues, and he told us to go ahead and ask him what it is that we wanted to know. And he said that he had no intention of repeating anything. And then these questions followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question, is it? You have put a whole suggestion to him involving identities of people, senior leading person from the Ministry of Interior or Ministry of Defence, suggesting to him and Bilobrk about planting rifles next to dead civilians. That is what you've done right at the start, according to this -- this note. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why isn't it recorded in this Official Note that you originally asked him questions about what he did and he declined to answer them? Why isn't it in this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't have an explanation for that. But it was really not relevant for the interview itself. We were specifically interested in this: There seemed to be a constant tug between what they knew and what they didn't know, and we were just trying to establish what knowledge they actually had. Because in the previous two interviews, both Mr. Vrticevic and Bilobrk told to our colleague Mr. Badzim -- or, rather, they declined. They did not wish to cooperate. They declined to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So they could have given information on a wide range of matters concerning their activities in relation to Grubori, what they had done on the 27th of August; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You would have been interested in -- in many aspects because you were investigating Grubori as a general criminal investigation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As forensic technicians who attend the crime scene, you would have also been investigating why there was no on-site investigation at Grubori by a judge, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Of course. When speaking about on-site investigations, that would be the case. But here, it was not an on-site investigation; it was really sanitisation, removal of bodies. On-site investigation is something that, under our laws, has to be attended by both an investigating judge and a State Prosecutor and a team, a forensic team, and, on occasion, also forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're very familiar with that information. And you would have been aware that a on-site investigation had been requested by the chief of the Knin Police Administration, Cedo Romanic, to investigate what had happened in Grubori. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We heard about it during our investigation. That fact was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a judge had been requested by Mr. Romanic. And were you aware whether a judge was delayed in attending the scene at Grubori for an on-site investigation on the 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These men were involved in human sanitation, but that did not prevent them in being part of an on-site investigation taking place with an investigating judge, did it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no on-site investigation in Grubori, according to what we were able to establish during our crime investigation of that event. It was just a human sanitisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I was about to ask you what you really asked the witness in your previous question, but I thought it wiser first it wait for his answer. The question is ambiguous as whether it would factually prevent them, whether it would legally prevent them, and apparently the witness says there was no on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was, for me -- I would have asked for a clarification if I were a witness, which I'm not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, in relation to what these men knew as to what happened on the 27th of August, there were many questions you could have asked them, isn't that right, as to what they knew?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. But many of those questions had already been answered and clarified through prior interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Vrticevic here, when you went to interview him, you did not tell him, did you, that this was an official interview. You just turned up at the police station and told him this was an informal chat.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. No, that is not true. Our arrival at the police administration, the Split-Dalmatia administration, and the need to conduct interviews with Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk, was announced by the chief of the MUP. They were -- had been informed. Now, whom he had contacted, I really don't know. We did not go there on our own initiative. That was the rule, that if a matter involves policemen from another administration, that one of the superiors would have to inform their superiors of a -- the arrival of interviewers and the need to conduct an interview with them. So you couldn't really say that we were there unofficially. We had a travel order issued to us to travel to Split. We were given an official vehicle for that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But with all that official background, when you saw Vrticevic, you just said it was for an informal chat, didn't you? Simply that.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Without any notes being taken at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, again, this question is ambiguous. Was it that they would have said that no notes would be taken or that no notes were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm -- I'm relying on my English intuition, that one follows the other. And I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there were no notes taken at the time that you saw him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I myself did not take any notes of this interview with Mr. Vrticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Neither did your colleague, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Then it was -- the notes were taken by my colleague Mr. Gerovac, if it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What this Official Note also records of your conversation with Mr. Vrticevic is that you suggested the names Zeljko Sacic or General Cermak being responsible for the suggestion to plant weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a question that was specifically put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was not what Franjo Djurica had told you, was it? Either Zeljko Sacic or General Cermak. Franjo Djurica didn't tell you that, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurica did not mention Mr. Sacic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he didn't say, according to you, that General Cermak had certainly or definitely suggested the planting of weapons, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurica said that what he had been told by Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk in that conversation, that it had been suggested by General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we have a look at what you told the Prosecutor in a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have a 65 ter number on this, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Hedaraly can help you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is -- sorry. It is 65 ter 7669. It was on our exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm much obliged. If we could have that document and go to, first of all, the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a statement that has been taken by you -- from you. We have an English copy. And there's a copy in your own language, which has been signed by you, Mr. Mikulic. Do you recognise your signature on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom of the page, please. It's signed in English as well, I think. In the Croatian version -- in the English version there. And if we can go to the last page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see your signature there with the date of the 3rd of March, 2010?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. This is not my signature on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have the page before that, please. Sorry, my mistake. Page 3. If we can just go down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go to paragraph 4 of the statement. If we go down the Croatian page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you read paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to the foot of the page, please. Paragraph 4. The other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a hard copy available somewhere? Because it seems to be a -- there we are. There we are. Could you please read what you find in paragraph 4 on the bottom, and once you have finished this page, to tell us, so that we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. What I'm asking you about is what you say he told you, that he came: "... to learn that on the day the bodies were collected, there were proposals by high-level officials in the field that the scene of the killings be orchestrated in such a way that weapons would be placed next to the victims to make it appear they died in armed conflict. Franjo did not name any of these high-level officials. I asked him who they were, and he responded ... most probably, it was General Cermak." Do you stand by this statement as something Franjo Djurica said to you? Do you say he said that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Weren't you interested to find out who the high-level officials were, in the plural?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, when Mr. Djurica said what he did, after that, we did not have any more questions. He told us that whatever he said basically was all that he was able to say at that -- at the moment and that did he not intend to stay anything about what Mr. Bilobrk and Vrticevic had said to me, that he was not going to go into any further details. And that's how the conversation ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he wouldn't name any of these high-level officials. And you asked him who they were. And he responded: "...most probably, it was General Cermak." So would you agree, from that, he is not saying that he knew it was General Cermak on your account?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. He spoke based on what was said to him by Bilobrk and Vrticevic. I apologise, you will probably remember that I said, in response to the Prosecutor's questions, that Mr. Bilobrk and Vrticevic's statements and finally Mr. Djurica's statements were taken with a grain of salt because there's a lot of contradiction among them, and they don't seem to be conclusive, either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, even taking that into account, why did you say to Mr. Vrticevic, as we've seen on Exhibit P2735, that -- whether someone from the then-senior leading structures had suggested to him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: From the higher structures of the MUP or -- we already had information when all that was happening, when the sanitisation was being organised, together with the departure for Grubori, that General Cermak was there, that Mr. Sacic was there, and others. That had already been established during the crime investigation. We also knew that Mr. Sacic was with a team that went to Grubori to carry out the sanitisation. We already knew that. Mr. Sacic even drove a car to Grubori. He drove his own official car, and his passengers were Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk. At least that's what Mr. Vrticevic and Bilobrk stated. And I believe that Mr. Sacic also confirmed that. I wasn't the one who spoke to Mr. Sacic, but I believe that he confirmed that he drove a car to Grubori to the crime scene. And that is why, while we interviewed Mr. Vrticevic, we felt we could ask him very specifically whether the proposal came from Mr. Cermak or from Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you didn't know, according to the information from Franjo Djurica, where these proposals exactly were made, who by, what level of high officials. You didn't know any of that information, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Djurica said that the proposal most probably, according to what he had been told in the interview with Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk, that the proposal had most probably come from General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your interview with -- with Vrticevic, he denied that that possibility had happened; at first, categorically, you said. Isn't that right, even on your account?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Could I please see the Official Note. But even without it, I believe that that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will read it out. "The interviewed person at first categorically denied such a possibility, but after a short time, he said he was not able to remember exactly. But he did allow the possibility that at that time someone might have suggested something like that."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Even though he denied this categorically, you tried to get him to change his story, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. He said all that in one breath. Within the scope of one sentence he said all that. Why he chose to change his position, I don't know. That's the way he spoke. That's the way he expressed himself. And that's how it was recorded in the Official Note. And that's why I said that all those Official Notes are full of contradictions. And that's why we took them with a grain of salt during our official investigation. If you compare Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic's statements, you will see that there are a lot of contradictions. It looked to us as if they were trying to divert us, to point us in a wrong direction. And that's why we were mistrustful of those statements. We did not consider them very credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, why did you then go on to suggest the names of Sacic or Cermak? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, during our crime investigation, we had already learned who was present during the sanitisation in Grubori, who were the persons who had arrived in the Knin Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next exhibit I want to look at is P2732, which is the Official Note with Mr. Bilobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From this record, it seems that you did not ask Mr. Bilobrk any general questions about what he was doing on the 27th of August; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I believe that on the second page you will see his words by way of explanation, that he had -- actually, during previous interviews, he provided a lot more details about that, about what he did and how he acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the fact that, according to this record, you suggested to him that there had been a plan or a suggestion made to plant guns next to the bodies of dead civilians. That was something that you said and suggested to him was what had happened.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, we did not suggest anything. Our questions were very concrete, very specific. At least that's how you will see it worded in the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it seems to start here that he was informed of the need to repeat the preliminary interview. Do you agree it says that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have the first page on the screen. I only have the second page, but my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then you said to him that there were new facts which suggested he didn't provide all the facts in his possession regarding that event.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that he was asked if it had been suggested to him and to his colleague, Vrticevic, and it goes on to say about someone in the MUP or MO [sic], that they should have conducted an on-site investigation and placed guns next to the bodies. So on -- on this note, it seems you are presenting the whole picture to him. You weren't asking him questions at all. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: The question was worded as it was. Some people may find it leading, but it was a very concrete question, a very specific question. We did not have to start from scratch. We did not have to start from the general aspects in order to narrow things down to the concrete. We started with the concrete things immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before we end up in a lengthy debate about what is a suggestion, what is -- it's clear, I think I asked questioned about this as well, that this was not spontaneously told by the witness but that it was put to him that this was the information apparently available by the persons who interviewed them and that they're asking, apparently, for confirmation. And that is certainly leading. Whether it's suggesting depends on the specific way in which the question was put. Did you, at the end, once you had put all this to the witness, did you say, Is this true or not true; or did you say, Is it true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we didn't say that at all. We didn't ask him if things were true or not. Whatever he said, that was the end of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you put all this information you had to him. What did you then ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never told him or made him guess whether we agreed with anything or not. We just wanted him to give us his own version of the events in his own words. We never even tried to make him aware of our opinion. That was his own opinion. It was taken into account. It was the information that he was privy to. And -- they were taken -- that was taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we're ending up in a kind of a debate which doesn't assist us greatly. It appears to me that, on the basis of what you just said, that it was put to him that you had information of the following nature, of the following content, and that you were seeking his comment on that. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I think, whether we call it suggestion or putting it to someone, that's a matter which seems to be a -- not the core of the problem. The issue apparently is: Did someone come up spontaneously with information --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when asked by open questions, or does someone confirm, apart from what have been the previous story about interviews and reluctance or non-reluctance to give any answers, but whether this was, as I said, mentioned first by the interviewer or first by the interviewed person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether we call it suggestion or not, unless you consider that it's important to find a common linguistic denominator for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm happy this point has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd taken it as far as it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, I am putting to you that Jozo Bilobrk never said that General Cermak had suggested the placing of guns by the dead bodies at Grubori to make it seem as though there been an armed conflict. I'm making it clear to you that he never said that. What's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know why he would claim that. What I'm say is that he did state that. Why he is now changing his statement - if what you are saying is true, with all due respect - I don't know. I don't understand. He -- he should be asked that. He is the one who should give you an answer to that. I state with full responsibility that what you read in the Official Note faithfully reflects what he stated during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that you went there to interview these two on this day, to see if you could get an account against General Cermak. That's the reason why you went there.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. No way. I apologise. We were primarily interested in the crime investigation about the perpetrators of the crime in Grubori. All the other things were said by the way, during that interview. Those things were just a byproduct of the interview. We made them aware during the interview that we are dealing with serious things and that one of the charges in the indictment was the crime in Grubori. We wanted them to realise the seriousness of the conversation, the seriousness of the situation. We invited them not to try to cover up for their own private interests. We invited them to present the objective situation, to give us all the facts that they had, that it was not either up to them or to us to make any decisions, any final decisions, on what had happened. At that point, we'd made them realise that we were interested in the objective facts of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you didn't ask him for the objective facts of what happened, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was something missing in the interpretation from the answer. Probably due to the speed of speech not intentional by anyone. But the word "vazno" was part of the answer, and that was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does it fit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Line 7, page 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to you -- I read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That sentence, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "We invited ..." That sentence? The sentence starting with "We invited ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "That it was not ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Mr. Kuzmanovic thinks that perhaps not everything has been translated you said. I'll read to you what was translated. And if anything is missing, please tell us. Part of your answer was: "...that it was not either up to them or to us to make any decisions, any final decisions, on what had happened." Does that completely reflect your answer, or is something missing? That portion of your answer, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "That it was not either up" -- And now it disappears from our screen. I apologise. I'll get it back. I re-start: "...that it was not either up to them or to us to make any decisions, any final decisions, on what had happened." Is anything missing in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I explain? May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kuzmanovic thinks that one word is missing. Now I don't know how important it is, Mr. Kuzmanovic. You also know that we can check the original audio if there is any problem. If it's a minor matter, I suggest that we move on. If it is a more important matter, then we should further explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought, in my understanding, if I may say what I thought I heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless it is a vital part of the answer then, of course, you're supposed not to give any suggestions, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the portion that was not translated was: It was not up to us or up to them to determine what was important or not important. I believe that was missing from the answer and that the witness did state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've heard the comment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I said that it was neither up to us or up to them whether something was important or not, whether they were supposed to say something as opposed to something that they shouldn't say. What they were required to do was to present the objective truth, the truth as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you check this story that he gave you? Did you check it? Did you check whether he met General Cermak in Knin, sitting on the stairs with several colleagues? Did you investigate whether those colleagues existed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. We did not particularly dwell upon that. We didn't deal with that. I -- I don't know if anybody else checked that. I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you check whether he met General Cermak in Knin on that day, whether that event actually happened in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I believe that that information arose from the other interviews that had been carried out, both prior to the interview with him and after the interview with him. And that it was confirmed, based on those interviews, that Mr. Cermak -- or General Cermak, rather, was there on the day in the same police station. And that he was also in Grubori when -- after the sanitisation process was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you check where Bilobrk went on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Doing his job in his workplace, according to what we know. He is an employee of the police administration of Split and Dalmatia; however, at that time, he was borrowed by the police administration of Zadar or, rather, the police station of Knin as a crime technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you check with the civilian protection officers who would have worked with him on that day where he went?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I can't talk about those details, but checks were carried out. I was not the one doing the checks --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of background noise in the courtroom. The interpreter cannot hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpreter] The logic of the job imposes all those things to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down because the interpreters cannot follow you. And apart from that, there is some background noise as well. Could you please -- you were asked whether you checked where Bilobrk went on that day, and you said: "Doing his job in his workplace, according to what we know. "I don't [sic] talk about those details, but checks were carried out. I was not one doing the checks --" And could you please resume your answer on from that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that those checks were indeed carried out, but it was somebody else who carried them out, not myself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why -- why those checks were not made by you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, there's no special reason. It could have been either me or somebody else. Anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I asked the question because you reviewed the work of Mr. Badzim and his interviews with Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk, in which the planting of guns is not mentioned, so you reviewed the quality of his investigation. Did you have a discretion as to whether to carry out further checks on the statement of Bilobrk?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. The analysis of all those writings was done by the heads of the team, the head of the task force. I was an operative, and my task was different. I was -- I was told what to do, to do this or that, that I was supposed to check something or go somewhere to carry out an interview, and things like that. The entire team, the entire task force, numbered about seven, eight, or nine people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock. How much time would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have too much more, but it would be a good idea if could I reflect over the adjournment, Your Honour, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could I ask the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Depending on what goes on, Your Honour, probably 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. That's clear. We'll have a -- no, before we have the break. Mr. Hedaraly, is there any reason to believe that the next witness will take considerably more or less time than the present witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would think slightly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slightly less. Which means that there is a fair chance that we would complete all the testimony scheduled today. Before we take a break, I would like to inform the parties that the Chamber, for any further witnesses to be heard, has, on its mind, to use Thursday, the 10th, and Friday, the 11th of July [sic], for that. Mr. Kay, I think you were not available on witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think you meant June, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, yes, I -- time flies, isn't it? But not that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful for that. Your Honour knows there's an issue of travel documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, and I wondered whether that -- whether there is a risk that it will not be resolved. Whatever the Tribunal can do, of course, will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's probably more than we can do, and we -- we try to make our checks, and the people are contacted regularly. And as soon as they get the information, they're under instructions to contact my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it's out of our hands, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, I do -- I do understand that. But provided that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- travel documents will be there, there's no problem if we would proceed on Thursday, the 10th, or Friday -- and Friday, the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I'm grateful for the Court's accommodation on the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we have another matter outstanding that we do not know yet whether we would have to schedule and to reserve any time for the Markac Defence. Could we at least insist that you give it a thorough thought whether or not you intend to call any further witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Most certainly, Your Honour. We will get that probably by the end of today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate to hear it as soon as possible. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And before we take the break, I have something else to add. We'll take a break of approximately one hour. During that break, you should not speak with anyone, whether known or unknown persons, about your testimony. You should not even contact anyone, not communicate in any way about your testimony, which will continue this afternoon. We resume at five minutes past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I saw that Mr. Kuzmanovic was on his feet, which seems to be an indication that you have no further questions. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, my estimate was given prior to knowing Mr. Kay would be finished, so I will be longer than 15 minutes but not longer than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mikulic. Mr. Mikulic, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 3rd of March, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 7669.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you some questions about that statement and related events. In paragraph 4 of this statement, you reference the interview had you with Djurica Franjo - excuse me - and you note during this interview: "I asked Franjo why he told Bilobrk and Vrticevic to advise him if they spoke to anyone and how any information they gave could be damaging to the generals." The first thing I wanted to refer back to, Mr. Mikulic, is the statement that you -- or the Official Note, two of them, which were taken by Mr. Badzim. The first of which was -- is marked as P2731, 13th of October of 2009; the second of which is P2730, the 20th of October, 2009. Now, in P2731 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could get that up on the screen, on the second page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll ask you the question, Mr. Mikulic. You'll have a chance to review the document once it comes on the screen, if something's unclear. The portion of this particular Official Note states: "They also would like to emphasise that the Defence team asked to be notified of any subsequent requests for information regarding the talk that they had." And the second sentence following that states: "Because of the circumstances in which they gave their statements to the Defence team about a month ago, Vrticevic and Bilobrk declined to describe the clearing of terrain in the village of Grubori in detail as it could damage the generals." Now, in this Official Note, as I read this Official Note of the 13th of October, 2009, there is no mention that Franjo Djurica told Bilobrk and Vrticevic that any information they gave could be damaging to the generals, as you state in your OTP statement. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I know it's not on the screen right now due to some technical problem, but -- I mean, Mr. Kuzmanovic skipped two sentences. And the witness should at least be able to see the whole portion that's being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the witness should be able to see that. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't have a problem with that. It is my cross-examination though, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you need me to re-ask my question, Mr. Mikulic, or ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Could you, please? I wasn't able to follow since I didn't have this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problem. The question basically surrounds what you said in your OTP statement, the very first sentence, in which you state in your OTP statement that you asked Franjo why he told Bilobrk and Vrticevic to advise them if they spoke to anyone and how any information they gave could be damaging to the generals. And my question to you is, In the statement of -- or in the Official Note of the 13th of October of 2009, P2731, there is no mention of pressure put on Vrticevic and Bilobrk by Mr. Djurica. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: When reading Mr. Badzim's Official Note, in the first paragraph, I can see that it says they would specifically like to point out that the Defence team told them that any statement that might be sought from them subsequently and which would relate to the interview or conversation held with them, that they should be informed of it accordingly, which means that Mr. Vrticevic -- that Mr. -- Mr. Bilobrk was asked -- and Mr. Vrticevic were asked to inform them of any contact made with them with a view to taking statements from them. And this was something that they confirmed later on in conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I understand that. And that is correct. But my question was: Nothing in this Official Note of October 13th, 2009, states that either Mr. Vrticevic or Mr. Bilobrk were pressured to decline to discuss the matter in Grubori by Mr. Djurica; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, Mr. Mikulic, that Mr. Vrticevic never met with Mr. Djurica nor with the Defence team of General Markac at any time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the Official Note of the 20th of October, 2009 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P2370 - if we could get that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Also an Official Note taken by your colleague Mr. Badzim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why I don't have anything up on my screen. I don't know if it's the same for everyone, Your Honour, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had something else on my screen, but now I have a document which seems to be a supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 2730; my dyslexia again. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. That's probably why the screen's blank. 2730, P2730. Mr. Registrar, I don't have anything on my screen. It's black. So I don't know if my screen's not working or ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I may provide hard copy, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please. To the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, we're going to get you a copy - obviously it's not on your screen - so can you follow along with my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, you will see on the first page the date of the Official Note. And if you could refer to the last paragraph of this document, immediately prior to Mr. Badzim's signature. And, again, I'm referencing my proposition to you that Mr. Vrticevic never met with the Defence team of General Markac, including Mr. Djurica. I will read the last paragraph of the Official Note of Mr. Bilobrk, P2730. "He was asked by the general's Defence team in August this year to make a statement on the clearing up of the terrain in Grubori, together with Ivica Bobanac. But since Bobinac was not present in Grubori, he did not make any statements. The interview focussed solely on the Grubori event, and there was no discussion of any other events." Mr. Mikulic, had you careful reviewed the Official Notes, you would have noted that it was Mr. Bobinac who met with the Defence team along with Mr. Bilobrk and not Vrticevic, and that Mr. Vrticevic happened to be on vacation and was unavailable to be interviewed. Did you speak with Mr. Bobinac at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Vrticevic at any time whether he was interviewed by any member of the Markac Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I think this came up as a question in the interview. I can't be sure, but I think so. In -- from the Official Notes of my colleague Badzim, one could conclude - if we can trust what he wrote, and I don't have any reason to doubt it - that this was discussed, that he was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my proposition that Mr. Vrticevic was not interviewed or spoken to in any form by any member of the Markac Defence team; it's not possible, correct, for anyone to pressure him to discuss anything relating to Grubori from the Markac Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, does the fact that Mr. Vrticevic was not involved in any way in a discussion with the Markac Defence team -- did you do anything to determine whether or not Mr. Vrticevic did, in fact, meet with the Markac Defence team? That's, perhaps, a better question.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't try and verify this additionally. And I can't say if somebody else did it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because in your statement in paragraph 2, you do note the OTP statement, 65 ter 7669, about both Bilobrk and Vrticevic. "They had been previously interviewed by Djurica Franjo on behalf of the Defence teams for the generals." From where did you get that information, specifically related to Vrticevic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: From the Official Note - that's to say, from the first interview with Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic - made by Colleague Badzim. That was the first information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now when you interviewed Mr. Djurica and took his Official Note, dated 30th of October of 2009, which was -- in the English version, it's seven pages long; and in the Croatian version, it's four pages long. The last paragraph of this Official Note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first. Unless there is some wrong number or something of the kind, I would prefer that Mr. Kuzmanovic first phrases his question and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was simply going to suggest that -- I know there's technical difficulties, but if things are going to be read to the witness from documents that are in evidence, that he should be given an opportunity to follow along as well while it's being translated. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that a hard copy will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that at all, Your Honour. Obviously we didn't expect that this would -- the system would crash. And I don't walk around with unmarked extra copies of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about P2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that be printed out so that the witness has a ... I note that the e-court system in itself works so that we have access to the document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. I would note that, since this is a Prosecution witness, if the Prosecution does have extra copies available that are blank ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have B/C/S copies. But we asked for some. So as soon as we get them, we'll notify -- I think we just received the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic, otherwise a tiny little piece of paper with the numbers would assist the Registrar in already preparing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you come to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The only documents we planned on using were the documents that were marked identified by the Prosecution. So any documents that are there ... on that list. I know the Court doesn't get that list, but I believe the Registrar does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have ... have hard copies been provided of all of the documents now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We are just checking to make sure they're the right exhibits. As soon as we confirm that, we'll give a copy to Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you would always clearly indicate what P number we're talking so we can get it on our screens --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and be able to follow. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulic, in front of you is the Official Note of Mr. Djurica. Before I start asking you some questions about it, the Court and -- here in this matter has heard a great deal about Official Notes, and you yourself mentioned in your direct testimony that Official Notes themselves are something that are not considered to be evidence and that there are things in Official Notes that obviously have been in dispute in this case. The last paragraph of this particular Official Note, where it's written: "In the rest of the interview, Djurica Franjo did not have anything to state concerning the above-stated circumstances and was unable to provide any other information of operative interest." If a court in Croatia were to read this document and that last paragraph, it is, in fact, not true that Djurica Franjo was unable to provide any other information of operative interest. Is that correct? Because you omitted, if it's true, a significant item that Mr. Djurica and you discussed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. I apologise, I wouldn't agree with you. I have already said that Mr. Djurica pointed out in the introductory part of the interview we held with him that what he was going to say had to be divided into a period leading up to 1995 and into a period when he joined the commission for the Defence of the general. And, therefore, a distinction had to be drawn between the information he came by up until 1995 and the information he came by as part of his work for the commission of which he did not wish to state anything. The very note follows the chronology as it was back in 1995, and, therefore, based on the position he expressed at the outset, we discussed that period alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But my question was related to this: The last part of the last sentence of the Official Note states: "... and was unable to provide any other information of operative interest." That statement is false; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: As far as this particular part of the interview is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And a court in Croatia many times reviews these documents and makes decisions on whether to prosecute or not to prosecute based on information provided in Official Notes, does it not? In part.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No. Official Notes made by police officers are excluded from the case file, and it cannot be adduced as evidence under the Croatian laws.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone, please, because the interpreters have difficulties in following your speech. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you provide this information that you claim Mr. Djurica told you to any judicial body in Croatia, any investigative body in Croatia, in written form?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: If we forwarded it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: This Official Note was forwarded as part of the criminal report which was subsequently filed. I don't know if it was forwarded as supporting documentation. I can't claim that with certainty. But I think that it should be part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about the part that you told Mr. Djurica that he allegedly told you after you said you wouldn't include it in the Official Note. Was that discussion in any written form provided to any court or official organ in Croatia related to this case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to the question. The Official Note concerning that particular information was written. And whether it was forwarded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had, in your role investigating this case, any interviews or meetings with Mr. Cetina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the events, he was the chief of the crime police in the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, was he not, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that from the file itself. But I've never met him, and I've never interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why Mr. Cetina was not interviewed by your office relating to the Grubori case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't answer the question. Mr. Cetina is still employed with the ministry. I know that much, but I don't know if he was interviewed as part of this criminal investigation. I suppose that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the ones to interview him other than you or Mr. Gerovac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that there were more of us in the task force or in the Working Group, and it could -- the interview could have been conducted by some of the higher-positioned officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Ivo Kardum who was the chief of the crime police in Zadar. Was he interviewed by your office at the time of the events?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: Do you mean last year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MIKULIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain. Unfortunately, I cannot provide an answer. I did not interview him personally, and I don't know whether anyone else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Vrkic from the police station in Knin? Do you know who that is, who was there at the time of the events, that there should be a terrain clearing?
